summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It holds full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands, which sits as the Kingdom's apex court, and it has its own Criminal Code, enacted in 2011.

Same-sex sexual activity between men and between women is legal, and the age of consent is 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse alike. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would class as same-sex therefore faces no conduct offence.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Curaçao since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld an Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Before that ruling the island was required, as part of the Kingdom, to recognise as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, while offering no in-island marriage, civil union or other form of recognition. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status can now marry locally. The ruling rests on sexual-orientation discrimination, and its reach into gender-identity grounds is not established by the sources.

The 2011 Criminal Code prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including "heterosexual or homosexual orientation". Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any distinction affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other fields of social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year's imprisonment. The grounds enumerated are sexual orientation; gender identity is not among them.

Official positions have not been uniform. In April 2015 representatives of all four Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights quickly, and Curaçao's commissioner at the time, Marvelyne Wiels, publicly backed equal rights for everyone. A party colleague, Winifred Raveneau, opposed that position and in 2013 used an exceptionally strict last-minute permit to force Curaçao's Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel.
tangentialFactors:
Aruba, a neighbouring constituent country of the Kingdom, passed same-sex civil partnerships on 8 September 2016. The measure does not extend to Curaçao.

Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag has cited an award from the International LGBTQ+ Travel Association naming Curaçao the most gay-welcoming destination in the region. The claim is an advocacy accolade rather than a measure of conditions on the ground.

In April 2015 a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague, the seat of the Kingdom government.

Curaçao, with Aruba and Sint Maarten, has been described as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom as a whole.
localsOnly:
The route to local marriage recognition ran through Kingdom-level politics and litigation. In August 2015 the European Court of Human Rights ruling in Oliari and Others v. Italy, applicable to Curaçao, required legal recognition of same-sex relationships. A limited-rights proposal went to the Estates in 2017, and a marriage bill submitted on 4 June 2019 was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support.

Curaçao opened an LGBT community centre, the Pink House, in 2010.
outOfScopeNotes:
No gender-recognition or identity-document marker rules for trans people in Curaçao appear in the available sources; the position on changing name or gender marker on Curaçao documents is not sourced.

No trans-specific violence data, hate-crime enforcement statistics, or police practice on anti-trans incidents is recorded for Curaçao.

No law or practice on access to toilets, changing rooms or other single-sex facilities is recorded.

No rules on access to hormone therapy, surgery or other transition-related care for visitors or residents are recorded.

Whether the Criminal Code's discrimination and incitement provisions have been applied to gender-identity-based conduct or speech is not documented.
